newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenyan capital calm at start of strike day.
newsitem.headline: Kenyan capital calm at start of strike day.

text.p: The centre of the Kenyan capital was calm on Friday morning but most shops were closed fearing violence and looting during a one-day national strike called by opposition groups.
Many workers, perhaps fearing penalties after the government declared the strike unlawful, ignored the protest to back demands for pre-election political reforms from President Daniel arap Moi.
Traffic in Nairobi was thinner than usual but buses were running and work continued almost normally on building sites and in government offices.
Trading began on time in the shilling currency which sank to an historic low against the dollar on Thursday because of growing political uncertainty ahead of elections which must be held this year.

The 73-year-old leader, in power since 1978, wants a final five-year term but the opposition insists on reforms to prevent rigging by the ruling Kenya African National Union (KANU) and civil servants.
Strike advocates in the divided opposition won no support in Friday's newspapers including the independent Daily Nation.
"The strike which has been called for today is not the best method of pressing home the need for constitutional reform," the Nation said in an editorial.
It said workers who stayed at home were as likely to be fearful for their security as showing support for the strike.
At least nine people were killed on July 7 when security forces suppressed pro-reform protests in Nairobi and other centres.
Previous protests have degenerated into looting by the unemployed and hordes of street children with shopkeepers of Asian origin the favourite targets.
"I think most of the Nairobi centre will be closed. The Asians will not be opening. As you know when two elephants fight it is the grass that gets hurt," an Asian businessman told Reuters on Friday.

The strike was called by the National Convention Executive Committee (NCEC), an umbrella reform group which wants sweeping changes to the constitution and the repeal of numerous laws before the elections.
Moi has offered limited concessions on those issues, splitting an opposition already divided on ethnic lines.
The level of backing for the protest will be an acid test both for the NCEC and for a government weakened by a run on the currency, labour unrest and corruption scandals.
The NCEC called for rallies in Nairobi's Uhuru park and in 11 provincial towns later on Friday.
Kenya's second city, the Indian Ocean port of Mombasa, was quiet with shops and businesses open, a Reuters correspondent there reported.
He said there was a heavy police presence on Mombasa streets unlike in Nairobi where men of the feared para-military General Service Unit (GSU) were apparently being held in reserve.
The shilling has lost more than 18 percent since the International Monetary Fund (IMF) halted a $205 million aid package a week ago, citing the government's failure to crack down on corruption.
Moi won some respite when air traffic controllers agreed on Thursday to suspend a five-day go-slow which brought chaos to passenger and cargo flights.
